title: Captain Cook's first voyage
subtitle: Science, stars and a new map of the Pacific, 1768–1771

intro.title: A voyage disguised as science
intro.story: In 1768 the Royal Society sent James Cook and the ship Endeavour to the Pacific for a scientific mission: to observe the planet Venus crossing the face of the Sun from the island of Tahiti. But Cook also carried secret orders — to search the southern ocean for the rumoured great continent, and to claim useful lands for Britain. Aboard were astronomers, artists and the botanist Joseph Banks.

stop.title: Round the Horn
stop.story: The Endeavour crossed the Atlantic and rounded Cape Horn, the storm-lashed southern tip of South America, rather than risk the Spanish-controlled route through Magellan's strait. Cook was a brilliant navigator and a stubborn enforcer of shipboard cleanliness and fresh food, determined to beat the scurvy that killed so many sailors on long voyages.

stop.title: The transit of Venus
stop.story: The Endeavour reached the lush island of Tahiti in good time. There, on 3 June 1769, the astronomers watched Venus cross the Sun — measurements that helped work out the true distance from the Earth to the Sun. The Tahitian priest and navigator Tupaia joined the ship, his deep knowledge of Pacific islands and stars proving invaluable.

stop.title: Charting New Zealand
stop.story: Sailing south and west, Cook reached New Zealand and spent six months charting its coasts with astonishing accuracy, proving it was two large islands, not part of a southern continent. His crew met the Māori — encounters that ranged from cautious trade to deadly violence, a pattern that would shadow the whole voyage.

stop.title: The east coast of Australia
stop.story: Pressing west, the Endeavour became the first European ship to chart the fertile east coast of Australia, landing at a bay so rich in new plants that Banks had it named Botany Bay. The land was already home to Aboriginal peoples who had lived there for tens of thousands of years. Cook's charts and his later claim of the coast for Britain would, within two decades, bring British colonisation — with devastating consequences for those first peoples.

stop.title: Home, and a changed map
stop.story: The voyage nearly ended on the Great Barrier Reef, where the Endeavour was holed and barely saved. Fever caught in Batavia then killed many of the crew, including Tupaia. Cook reached England in July 1771 having lost no one to scurvy — a landmark in seafaring — and carrying charts, specimens and drawings that redrew the map of the Pacific and made him the most famous navigator of his age.

outro.title: Discovery and its shadow
outro.story: Cook's voyages opened the Pacific to European science — and to European empire. The same charts that advanced knowledge of the world's geography also guided the ships that colonised Australia, New Zealand and the Pacific islands, uprooting peoples who had lived there for millennia. Cook's story is a reminder that 'discovery' always has two sides, and that the lands he mapped were never truly empty.
